questions.prompt: State the similarity formula for changing the matrix of a linear map from basis B to basis C.
questions.answer: If A is the matrix of T in basis B and P converts C-coordinates to B-coordinates, then the matrix in basis C is \(P^{-1}\)AP. The rightmost P converts the input to B-coordinates, A applies the map, and \(P^{-1}\) converts the output back to C-coordinates.

First compute AP = \(\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\)\(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\). Now multiply by \(P^{-1}\): \(\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\)\(\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\). Therefore \(P^{-1}\)AP = \(\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: Why does \(P^{-1}\)AP have P on the right and \(P^{-1}\) on the left?
questions.answer: Matrix products act on coordinate columns from right to left. The rightmost P first converts the input coordinates from the new basis to the old basis. Then A applies the old-basis matrix. Finally \(P^{-1}\) converts the output back to the new basis. Therefore the correct order is \(P^{-1}\)AP.

First compute AP = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\)\(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\). Now compute \(P^{-1}\)AP = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\)\(\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\-2&-1\end{pmatrix}\). Therefore the changed-coordinate matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\-2&-1\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: If two matrices are similar, what do they represent geometrically or algebraically?
questions.answer: Similar matrices represent the same linear map written in different bases. The underlying transformation is unchanged; only the coordinate system used to describe inputs and outputs has changed.

questions.prompt: Show that similar matrices A and \(P^{-1}\)AP have the same determinant.
questions.answer: Use the product rule for determinants. \(\det(AP)\) = \(\det()\)\(\det(A)\)\(\det(P)\). Since \(\det()\) = 1/\(\det(P)\), this becomes (1/\(\det(P)\))\(\det(A)\)\(\det(P)\) = \(\det(A)\). Therefore similar matrices have the same determinant.

The matrix \(P_{B\leftarrowC}\) converts C-coordinates to B-coordinates. Compute [v]_B = \(P_{B\leftarrowC}\)[v]_C = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\)\((2,1)\). The result is \((1\cdot 2 + 1\cdot 1, 0\cdot 2 + 1\cdot 1)\) = \((3,1)\).

If \(P_{B\leftarrowC}\) = \(I_2\), then the two bases are the same for coordinate conversion. The similarity formula gives [T]_C = \(I_2\)^{-1}[T]_B \(I_2\) = [T]_B. Therefore [T]_C = \(\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&5\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: A matrix A has trace 4. If \(B=P^{-1}\)AP, what is the trace of B?
questions.answer: Similar matrices have the same trace. Since \(B=P^{-1}\)AP is similar to A and \(\operatorname{tr}(A)\) = 4, \(\operatorname{tr}(B)\) = 4.

questions.prompt: A learner writes the changed-coordinate matrix as PAP^{-1}. Diagnose the error.
questions.answer: The order depends on what P converts. If P converts new-basis coordinates to old-basis coordinates, then the correct formula is \(P^{-1}\)AP. The rightmost matrix must first convert the input into the coordinate system where A applies, and the leftmost matrix converts the output back. Writing PAP^{-1} reverses the conversion path and generally gives a different matrix.
